goals: Identify the Angas as Jain texts and the Tripitakas and the Jatakas as Buddhist texts

slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we know about two new faiths and why they arose.

nodes.label: Causes of new faiths in the 6th century BCE

slides.narration: In the sixth century before the common era, two new teachers, Mahavira and the Buddha, gained many followers in northern India. In this part we learn which texts tell us about their teachings, and why so many people were ready to listen.

visual.caption: The two founders on a timeline (approximate dates).

slides.narration: Look at the timeline. The Buddha is commonly taught as born about five hundred and sixty three before the common era, and Mahavira about five hundred and forty. Both fall in the sixth century. Books differ on exact dates, so we always say about.

slides.heading: Sources at a glance

rows: Twelve in tradition; compiled at Valabhi
Stories of the Buddha's earlier births

visual.alt: Table of sources: the Angas for Jainism, twelve in tradition and compiled at Valabhi; the Tripitakas for Buddhism, three baskets composed in Pali; and the Jatakas, stories of the Buddha's earlier births

slides.narration: Three groups of texts help us. The Angas are the sacred texts of Jainism. The Tripitakas are the sacred texts of Buddhism, composed in the Pali language. The Jatakas are Buddhist stories about the earlier births of the Buddha. In this chapter we need only a brief knowledge of each.

slides.heading: The Jain Angas
bullets: The **Angas** are sacred **Jain** texts, **twelve** in tradition.
The teachings were first **passed on orally**.
They were compiled at the **Council of Valabhi**, about the **fifth to sixth century CE**.

nodes.label: Teachings passed on by word of mouth
Council of Valabhi, about 5th to 6th century CE

visual.alt: Flow: Jain teachings were passed on orally, then compiled at the Council of Valabhi about the fifth to sixth century CE, giving the twelve Angas in tradition
visual.caption: How the Angas came to be written.

slides.narration: The Angas are sacred Jain texts, twelve in number according to tradition. For a long time the teachings were passed on by word of mouth. They were compiled at the Council of Valabhi, about the fifth to sixth century of the common era. Always say about when you give this date.

slides.heading: The Buddhist Tripitakas
bullets: Each Pitaka has its own subject.

rows: Rules of conduct for monks and nuns
Discourses and teachings attributed to the Buddha
Deeper philosophical analysis of the teachings

visual.alt: Table of the three Pitakas: the Vinaya Pitaka holds rules for monks and nuns, the Sutta Pitaka holds discourses of the Buddha, the Abhidhamma Pitaka holds deeper analysis

slides.narration: Tripitaka means three baskets. The Vinaya Pitaka holds rules of conduct for monks and nuns. The Sutta Pitaka holds discourses and teachings attributed to the Buddha. The Abhidhamma Pitaka holds deeper analysis of the teachings. All three were composed in the Pali language, which ordinary people could follow more easily than Sanskrit.

slides.heading: The Jatakas
slides.body_md: A **Jataka** is a story told as an **earlier birth of the Buddha**.

nodes.label: Told as earlier births of the Buddha
Glimpses of markets, villages and travellers

visual.alt: Flow: the Jatakas are stories told as earlier births of the Buddha, and they give glimpses of markets, villages and travellers
visual.caption: The Jatakas as a source.

slides.narration: The Jatakas are stories told as earlier births of the Buddha. Many of them are set among merchants, villagers and travellers, so they give historians glimpses of everyday life. Because they are stories, a historian reads them together with other sources.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the sources
slides.body_md: Match each source with its description.
slides.narration: Think about which texts are Jain and which are Buddhist. Then match the Vinaya and Sutta baskets with their contents.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing the right source
slides.body_md: Read the question, then name the source.
bullets: Step 1 — Is the question about Jainism or Buddhism?
Step 2 — Is it about rules, teachings or stories?
Step 4 — Add a caution if the text is a story.

rows: What rules did Buddhist monks and nuns follow?
What are the main Jain texts?
How did traders and villagers live?
What did the Buddha teach in his talks?

visual.alt: Table matching four historian questions with sources: Buddhist monastic rules in the Vinaya Pitaka, Jain texts in the Angas, traders and villagers in the Jatakas with other sources, and the Buddha's talks in the Sutta Pitaka

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. First decide whether the question is about Jainism or Buddhism. Then decide whether it asks about rules, teachings or stories. Name the text that fits. Monastic rules go to the Vinaya Pitaka. Jain texts are the Angas. Stories of daily life are found in the Jatakas, to be read with care.

slides.heading: Why new faiths arose
slides.body_md: Historians point to **several causes** working together.

rows: Costly rituals; priests; Sanskrit not understood by many
Rigid varna system; Kshatriya and Vaishya aspirations
Cattle needed for farming; growth of trade and towns
Prakrit and Pali, close to common speech

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of cause for the rise of new faiths: religious, social, economic, political and language, each with a short description

slides.narration: Historians see several causes working together. Some were religious, some social, some economic and some political. The use of local languages also mattered. No single cause explains everything. In the next slides we look at each cause and at how to describe it fairly.

slides.heading: Religious causes
bullets: A **leading place** for priests in ceremonies.

rows: Sanskrit not understood by common people
Questioned some practices; the older tradition continued

visual.alt: Table of religious causes: complex and costly rituals, the leading place of priests, Sanskrit not understood by common people, and new teachers who questioned some practices while the older tradition continued

slides.narration: Over time, rituals and sacrifices had become complex and costly. Priests held a leading place in ceremonies, and the language of the rites, Sanskrit, was not understood by many ordinary people. The new teachers questioned some of these practices and offered other paths. The older tradition continued alongside them.

slides.heading: Social causes
bullets: **Kshatriyas** wanted a standing equal to their power.
**Vaishyas** were wealthy but wanted more respect.

rows: Rank was becoming fixed by birth
Wished for a standing equal to their power
Wealthy from trade but wanted more respect

visual.alt: Table of social causes: rank fixed by birth for all groups, Kshatriyas wishing for a standing equal to their power, and Vaishyas wealthy from trade but wanting more respect

slides.narration: In society, rank was becoming fixed by birth. Kshatriyas, the rulers and warriors, wished for a standing equal to their power. Vaishyas, who earned wealth from trade, wanted more respect than birth alone gave them. Teachings that valued conduct more than birth appealed to many groups.

slides.heading: Quick check: a villager's complaint
slides.body_md: Which cause does the villager's letter illustrate?
slides.narration: Read the letter again. The villager writes about costly rites and a language he cannot follow. Think about which kind of cause that is.

slides.heading: Economic causes
bullets: Farming needed **cattle**; large sacrifices used many animals.
Both groups found the new teachings **welcoming**.

visual.alt: Flow: farming needs oxen and cows, large sacrifices use many animals, so farmers welcomed the teaching of ahimsa
visual.caption: An economic cause: cattle.

slides.narration: Farming depended on oxen and cows, so large sacrifices that used up many animals worried farmers. They welcomed the teaching of ahimsa. At the same time, trade and towns were growing, and Vaishyas gained wealth. Many of them gave gifts to the new teachers and their followers.

slides.heading: Kingdoms and languages
slides.body_md: Rulers and local languages helped the new teachings **spread**.

rows: Larger kingdoms such as Magadha were growing
Rulers gave the new teachers gifts and protection
Prakrit and Pali reached many more people

visual.alt: Table of political and language points: larger kingdoms such as Magadha growing, rulers giving gifts and protection, and Prakrit and Pali reaching more people

slides.narration: Larger kingdoms, such as Magadha, were growing in this age. Rulers gave the new teachers gifts and protection, which helped the teachings spread. The teachers spoke Prakrit and Pali, languages close to everyday speech, so ordinary people could understand them directly.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classify the situation
slides.body_md: Sort each imagined situation under a kind of cause.
bullets: Step 1 — Read what the person says or does.
Step 2 — Ask: is it about rites, rank, money or rulers?

rows: A villager cannot follow the language of a long rite
A rich trader is ranked low because of birth
A farmer cannot spare an ox for a sacrifice
A king gives a rest-house to a teacher

visual.alt: Table sorting four imagined situations into causes: a villager who cannot follow a rite is religious, a rich trader ranked low by birth is social, a farmer who cannot spare an ox is economic, and a king giving a rest-house is political

slides.narration: Try this method. Read what the person says or does. Ask whether it is about rites, rank, money or rulers. Then name the cause and give a one line reason. A villager who cannot follow a long rite shows a religious cause. A rich trader ranked low by birth shows a social cause. A farmer who cannot spare an ox shows an economic cause.

slides.heading: Quick check: which entry does not belong?
slides.body_md: Find the entry that is NOT a cause.
slides.narration: Go through the causes you have just seen. Which entry on the list is not one of them?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) Three religious causes. [3] (ii) Two social causes and one economic cause. [3] (iii) Kingdoms and languages. [4]
bullets: One clear point for each mark.

rows: Two social causes and one economic cause
Kingdoms and royal support; local languages

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark answer on the causes: part (i) three religious causes for 3 marks, part (ii) two social causes and one economic cause for 3 marks, part (iii) kingdoms and local languages for 4 marks

slides.narration: To plan a ten mark answer in three parts, give three points to the first part, three to the second and four to the last. Part one gives three religious causes. Part two gives two social causes and one economic cause. Part three explains royal support and the use of local languages, with a closing line that the older tradition continued.

slides.heading: Quick check: cattle and ahimsa
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true.
slides.narration: Check each statement on its own first. Then ask whether the reason is correct.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: New teachings **questioned** some practices; the older tradition **continued**.

rows: Costly rituals; priests; Sanskrit not understood by many
Rigid varna system; Kshatriya and Vaishya aspirations
Cattle needed for farming; growth of trade and towns
Prakrit and Pali, close to common speech

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of cause for the rise of new faiths: religious, social, economic, political and language, each with a short description

slides.narration: To sum up. The Angas are Jain texts and the Tripitakas and Jatakas are Buddhist texts. New faiths arose in the sixth century before the common era because of religious, social, economic and political causes, and because teachers used the languages of the people. Describe all of this neutrally and respectfully.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Give **causes in kinds**: religious, social, economic, political.
Use **neutral words**: the teachings **questioned**, never insult any tradition.
Do not rank one faith above another.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Add the word about to every date. When you name a text, name its faith too. Group your causes into kinds. Use neutral words and say that the teachings questioned certain practices. Never insult any tradition, and never rank one faith above another.

slides.narration: This schematic map is not to scale. Lumbini is traditionally the birthplace of the Buddha. Bodh Gaya is where he attained enlightenment, and Sarnath is where he gave his first sermon. Kushinagar is where he passed away. Mahavira is said to have been born at Kundagrama near Vaishali.

slides.heading: Mahavira

rows: Vardhamana, later called Mahavira and Jina
About 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali
The twenty-fourth Tirthankara; Parshvanatha was the twenty-third
Kevala jnana, perfect knowledge, after years of austere practice

visual.alt: Table of facts on Mahavira: Vardhamana, later called Mahavira and Jina; born about 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali; the twenty-fourth Tirthankara after Parshvanatha; attained kevala jnana after years of austere practice

slides.narration: Vardhamana was born about five hundred and forty before the common era at Kundagrama near Vaishali. After years of austere practice he attained kevala jnana, or perfect knowledge. He was called Jina, the conqueror, and Mahavira, the great hero. Jains count him as the twenty fourth Tirthankara, after Parshvanatha.

slides.heading: The Tri-ratnas

visual.alt: Flow: right faith, right knowledge and right conduct, the Tri-ratnas, lead to moksha or liberation
visual.caption: The Tri-ratnas.

slides.narration: The three jewels, or Tri ratnas, are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. Right faith is trust in the teachings. Right knowledge is understanding them. Right conduct is living by them. Together they are the path that leads the soul towards moksha, or liberation.

slides.heading: Quick check: the three jewels
slides.body_md: Match the three actions of an imagined student with the Tri-ratnas.
slides.narration: Think about trusting, studying and living by the teachings. Match each with the correct jewel.

slides.heading: The five vows
bullets: Four vows were taught earlier by **Parshvanatha**.

rows: Not taking what is not given
Self-restraint; the fifth vow, added by Mahavira

visual.alt: Table of the five Jain vows: ahimsa not harming living beings, satya speaking the truth, asteya not taking what is not given, aparigraha limiting possessions, and brahmacharya self-restraint added by Mahavira

slides.narration: The five vows are ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya. Ahimsa is not harming any living being. Satya is truth. Asteya is not taking what is not given. Aparigraha is limiting attachment to possessions. Brahmacharya is self restraint. Parshvanatha taught the first four, and Mahavira added the fifth.

slides.heading: Karma, equality and moksha
bullets: **Equality**: every being has a soul; conduct, not birth, decides progress.
**Moksha**: freedom of the soul from karma.

nodes.label: Actions bind karma to the soul

visual.alt: Flow: actions bind karma to the soul, karma shapes rebirth, the Tri-ratnas and discipline shed karma, and the soul reaches moksha
visual.caption: Karma, rebirth and moksha in Jainism.

slides.narration: In Jain belief, actions bind karma to the soul, and karma shapes rebirth. The path to moksha, the freedom of the soul from karma, is followed through the three jewels and discipline. Jain teaching also holds that all living beings have souls, and that conduct, not birth, decides progress. Later, Jainism divided into two main sects, the Shvetambara and the Digambara.

slides.heading: The Buddha's life
slides.body_md: Siddhartha Gautama was born about **563 BCE** (dates vary).

visual.alt: Flow of four sites in the life of the Buddha: Lumbini for birth, Bodh Gaya for enlightenment, Sarnath for the first sermon and Kushinagar for mahaparinirvana
visual.caption: Four sites in the Buddha's life.

slides.narration: Siddhartha Gautama is traditionally said to have been born at Lumbini, about five hundred and sixty three before the common era; dates vary. After he left home to seek an answer to suffering, he attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath and passed away at Kushinagar, an event called mahaparinirvana.

slides.heading: The Four Noble Truths

rows: Desire is the cause of suffering
Suffering can come to an end
The Eightfold Path is the way

visual.alt: Table of the Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering, desire is the cause, suffering can come to an end, and the Eightfold Path is the way

slides.narration: The Four Noble Truths are the heart of the Buddha's teaching. The first truth is that life involves suffering. The second is that desire is the cause of suffering. The third is that suffering can come to an end. The fourth is that the Eightfold Path is the way to end it.

slides.heading: Quick check: which truth?
slides.body_md: Which Noble Truth does the imagined monk's teaching match?
slides.narration: Sickness, loss and old age are described. Think about which of the four truths speaks of these.

slides.heading: The Eightfold Path
slides.body_md: Eight steps; each begins with the word **right**.

visual.alt: Table of the eight steps of the Eightfold Path: right view, resolve, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration

slides.narration: The Eightfold Path has eight steps. They are right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. They guide a person in understanding, conduct and the training of the mind.

slides.heading: Quick check: order the steps
slides.body_md: Arrange four steps in their traditional order.
slides.narration: Recall the order from the table. Start with view and end with concentration.

slides.heading: The Middle Path, Nirvana and the Sangha
bullets: **Nirvana**: freedom from desire and from rebirth.

visual.alt: Flow: avoid extreme indulgence, avoid extreme self-denial, and follow the balanced Middle Path
visual.caption: The Middle Path.

slides.narration: The Middle Path avoids two extremes, extreme indulgence and extreme self denial. Nirvana is freedom from desire and from the cycle of rebirth, which brings suffering to an end. The Sangha, the community of monks and nuns, followed rules, preserved the teachings and helped to spread them.

slides.heading: Nirvana and the Sangha

nodes.label: Nirvana: suffering comes to an end

visual.alt: Flow: when desire ends, the cycle of rebirth ends, and Nirvana is the end of suffering
visual.caption: Nirvana.

slides.narration: When desire comes to an end, the cycle of rebirth comes to an end. This is Nirvana, the end of suffering. It is not a place or a kingdom. The Sangha, the community of monks and nuns, kept the teachings alive and shared them with ordinary people.

sections.heading: 1. Sources: the Angas, the Tripitakas and the Jatakas
sections.body_md:
- **Jain texts:** the **Angas**, twelve in tradition, handed down orally and compiled at the **Council of Valabhi**, about the 5th to 6th century CE (books differ).
- **Buddhist texts:** the **Tripitakas** (**Vinaya** Pitaka: rules for monks and nuns; **Sutta** Pitaka: discourses; **Abhidhamma** Pitaka: deeper analysis), composed in **Pali**.
- **Jatakas:** stories told as earlier births of the Buddha; many are set among merchants and villagers, so they give glimpses of daily life.
- A historian reads religious texts **with other sources**.

sections.heading: 2. Causes for the rise of new faiths in the 6th century BCE
sections.body_md:
- **Religious:** rituals and sacrifices had become complex and costly; priests had a leading place; Sanskrit was not understood by many people.
- **Social:** the varna system was becoming rigid; Kshatriyas and Vaishyas wished for a higher standing.
- **Economic:** farming needed cattle (ahimsa welcomed); trade and towns grew and Vaishyas gained wealth.
- **Political:** growth of kingdoms such as Magadha; rulers supported the new teachers.
- **Language:** Prakrit and Pali were close to everyday speech.
- The new teachings **questioned** some practices and offered other paths; the older tradition **continued**.

sections.heading: 3. Mahavira, the Tri-ratnas and the five vows
sections.body_md:
- **Vardhamana Mahavira:** born about **540 BCE** at **Kundagrama** near **Vaishali**; the **24th Tirthankara** (Parshvanatha was the 23rd); attained **kevala jnana** after austere practice; called **Jina** and **Mahavira**.
- **Tri-ratnas:** right faith, right knowledge, right conduct.
- **Five vows:** ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya (the fifth added by Mahavira).

sections.heading: 4. Karma, equality, moksha and later sects
sections.body_md:
- **Karma:** actions bind karma to the soul and shape rebirth.
- **Equality:** every living being has a soul; conduct, not birth, decides progress.
- **Moksha:** liberation of the soul from karma and the cycle of birth, through the Tri-ratnas and discipline.
- **Later sects (brief):** Shvetambara and Digambara.

sections.heading: 5. The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths
sections.body_md:
- **Siddhartha Gautama:** born about **563 BCE** at **Lumbini** (dates vary); **enlightenment** at **Bodh Gaya**; **first sermon** at **Sarnath**; **mahaparinirvana** at **Kushinagar**.
- **Four Noble Truths:** life involves suffering; desire is the cause; suffering can end; the Eightfold Path is the way.

sections.heading: 6. Eightfold Path, Middle Path, Nirvana, Sangha and comparison
sections.body_md:
- **Eightfold Path:** right view, resolve, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
- **Middle Path:** avoids extreme indulgence and extreme self-denial.
- **Nirvana:** freedom from desire and from the cycle of rebirth; the end of suffering.
- **Sangha:** the community of monks and nuns.
- **Similarities:** same century; questioned costly rituals; karma and rebirth; ahimsa; local languages; monastic orders.
- **Differences:** strict austerity and the Tri-ratnas with five vows (Jainism) versus the Middle Path, Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path (Buddhism); Buddhism spread to many lands.

- Confusing the Angas (Jain) with the Tripitakas and Jatakas (Buddhist).
- Mixing up the five vows with the Tri-ratnas.
- Listing only seven steps of the Eightfold Path, or confusing it with the Four Noble Truths.
- Writing that one faith is better than another, or insulting the older tradition.
- Quoting scripture instead of paraphrasing.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined diary, Meera writes that the librarian of a Jain temple library in the imagined town of Ratnapur showed her bundles of manuscripts and called them the Angas. What are the Angas?

options.text_md: The three baskets of Buddhist teaching, written in Pali
Sacred texts of Jainism, twelve in number according to tradition
Stories about the earlier births of the Buddha
Rules that applied only to the kings of Magadha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Sacred texts of Jainism, twelve in number according to tradition. The Angas are the Jain canon, twelve in tradition. The three baskets are the Tripitakas, the stories of earlier births are the Jatakas, and the Angas were not royal rules.

questions.stem_md: A card at an imagined school exhibition in Chandrapur reads: the part of the Buddhist canon that sets out rules of conduct for monks and nuns. Which Pitaka does it describe?

options.text_md: None of the three, since rules were never recorded

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Vinaya Pitaka. Rules of conduct for the monastic community belong to the Vinaya Pitaka. The Sutta Pitaka holds discourses and the Abhidhamma Pitaka deeper analysis, and rules were recorded.

questions.stem_md: A label at the imagined Vidya Mandir exhibition reads: tales in which a merchant, a monkey and a village headman appear, each told as an earlier birth of a great teacher. Which source does it describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Jatakas. Tales told as earlier births of the Buddha are the Jatakas. The Angas are Jain texts, the Vinaya Pitaka gives monastic rules, and the Abhidhamma Pitaka is deeper analysis, not stories.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A historian studying how traders and villagers lived in ancient times may find the Jatakas useful.

**Reason (R):** Many Jataka stories are set among merchants, villagers and travellers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Because many tales are set among ordinary people, they give glimpses of everyday life, which explains their usefulness.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A label at an imagined exhibition in Kaveripur says that the Jatakas are Jain texts which record the life of Mahavira.
questions.solution_md: **False.** The Jatakas are Buddhist stories of the Buddha's earlier births, not Jain texts about Mahavira.

questions.stem_md: A guide in the imagined library at Ratnapur says that the twelve sacred texts of the Jains, as counted in tradition, are called the ___.
questions.solution_md: The twelve Jain texts are the Angas.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined school exhibition, each card below must be paired with its description. Match them.

match_right.text_md: Rules of conduct for monks and nuns
Stories of the Buddha's earlier births
Sacred Jain texts, twelve in tradition
Discourses and teachings of the Buddha

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Angas are Jain; the Vinaya holds rules; the Sutta Pitaka holds discourses; the Jatakas are birth stories.

questions.stem_md: A student at the imagined Jain library in Ratnapur asks what the Angas are and when they were compiled. Answer in two points.
questions.solution_md: Jain texts; compiled at Valabhi.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Angas** form the Jain canon, **twelve** in the count of tradition. They were handed down by memory for generations and then written up at the **Council of Valabhi**, about the **fifth to sixth century CE**.

marking_scheme.step: Angas as sacred Jain texts, twelve in tradition
Compiled at Valabhi, about the 5th to 6th century CE

questions.stem_md: Name the three Pitakas of the Buddhist Tripitakas and say in a line what each holds. Mention the language of the texts.
questions.solution_md: Three Pitakas with contents.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Vinaya Pitaka:** rules of conduct for monks and nuns.
2. **Sutta Pitaka:** discourses and teachings attributed to the Buddha.
3. **Abhidhamma Pitaka:** deeper philosophical analysis of the teachings. The texts were composed in **Pali**.

questions.stem_md: Rudra, an imagined villager of Shravastipur, writes that a rite in his village now needs many priests, costly offerings and chants in a language none of the villagers follow. Which cause of the rise of new faiths does this illustrate best?

options.text_md: Economic: the arrival of coined money in the village markets
Political: the end of every kingdom in the region
Religious: complex and costly rituals, and a language ordinary people did not understand
Social: the abolition of all social groups

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Religious: complex and costly rituals, and a language ordinary people did not understand. Costly ceremonies and chants in a language the villagers could not follow are religious causes. Coins, the end of kingdoms or the abolition of social groups are not described in the letter.

questions.stem_md: Dhanapal, an imagined caravan trader of Chandrapur, has grown wealthy, yet he is told that his birth keeps him below others in rank. Which cause of the rise of new faiths does his situation show?

options.text_md: Religious: priests had stopped all ceremonies
Political: the king had ordered all traders to leave the town
Social: Vaishyas who gained wealth wanted a standing that birth alone did not allow
Economic: there was no trade in the towns

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Social: Vaishyas who gained wealth wanted a standing that birth alone did not allow. A rich trader held back by birth shows the social cause: the ambition of Vaishyas for higher standing. He is a trader in a trading town, so there was trade, and no ceremonies or royal order are mentioned.

questions.stem_md: Farmers in the imagined village of Gokulpur depend on their oxen to plough the fields and note that large sacrifices use up many animals. Which feature of the new teachings would appeal to them for economic reasons?

options.text_md: The stress on ahimsa, which discouraged killing animals
A rule that every household must offer animals
A rule that fields must never be ploughed
A demand that all wealth be given up at once

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The stress on ahimsa, which discouraged killing animals. An agricultural economy needed cattle, so the stress on ahimsa suited farmers. A duty to offer animals or a ban on ploughing would harm them, and giving up all wealth was not asked of householders.

questions.stem_md: A teacher in the imagined town of Kosalapur speaks in the everyday language of the region, not in Sanskrit. What was the likely effect?

options.text_md: The teaching was kept from ordinary people
Only the learned could follow the teaching
The teaching could not be remembered at all
More ordinary people could understand and follow the teaching

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** More ordinary people could understand and follow the teaching. Prakrit and Pali were close to common speech, so listeners understood directly. The other options reverse this effect.

questions.stem_md: A group project in an imagined Class IX lists causes of the rise of Jainism and Buddhism in the sixth century BCE. Which entry does NOT belong on the list?

options.text_md: The growth of trade and towns
A ban on farming imposed by every kingdom
Dislike of complex and costly rituals
Support from rulers of kingdoms such as Magadha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A ban on farming imposed by every kingdom. No such ban on farming is known; farming was growing. Trade and towns, dislike of costly rituals and royal support are all causes historians discuss.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined debate at the Kaveripur History Club, a speaker says that new faiths arose because the older religion had nothing of value. Which reply is the most accurate and respectful for a history answer?

options.text_md: These teachings questioned some practices and offered other paths, while the older tradition continued alongside them
The speaker is right, and the older tradition vanished in the sixth century BCE
The speaker is right, since only the new teachings valued non-violence
The speaker is wrong, since nobody then questioned any practice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** These teachings questioned some practices and offered other paths, while the older tradition continued alongside them. History records that the new teachers questioned certain practices and offered other paths, but the older tradition continued. The other replies overstate, disparage or deny the evidence.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The growth of trade and towns encouraged many Vaishyas to support the new teachings.

**Reason (R):** Prosperous Vaishyas wanted a standing that birth alone did not give them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Wealth from trade without matching social standing made Vaishyas welcome teachings that valued conduct, which explains their support.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Peasants in the sixth century BCE valued their cattle for ploughing and carrying loads.

**Reason (R):** The new teaching of ahimsa encouraged farmers to give their cattle away in sacrifice.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: ahimsa discouraged the killing of animals, which is why farmers found the teaching attractive.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an imagined class debate, a student says that Jainism and Buddhism rose in the sixth century BCE only for religious reasons, with no social or economic causes.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Historians point to religious, social, economic and political causes together, so the claim is false.

questions.stem_md: Jain teachers often used Prakrit, and the Buddhist texts were composed in a language of the people called ___.
questions.solution_md: The Buddhist canon was composed in Pali.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farmer and an imagined trader of the sixth century BCE both welcome the new teachings. State one economic reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Cattle for the farmer; trade and wealth for the trader.

answer.model_answer_md: **Farmer:** ploughing needed **cattle**, and the stress on **ahimsa** discouraged the killing of animals in large sacrifices. **Trader:** growing **trade and towns** brought wealth to Vaishyas, who gave gifts to the new teachers.

questions.stem_md: Why did the use of Prakrit and Pali, rather than Sanskrit, help the new teachings to spread?
questions.solution_md: Understood by common people.

answer.model_answer_md: Prakrit and Pali were close to the **everyday speech** of ordinary people, so they could **understand** the teachers directly. Sanskrit was understood mainly by the learned, so local languages **widened the audience**.

marking_scheme.step: Local languages understood by ordinary people

questions.stem_md: Ravi, in an imagined history club, lists religious causes for the rise of new faiths in the sixth century BCE. Give three points he could include.
questions.solution_md: Costly rites; priests; language.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Rituals and sacrifices had become **complex and costly**.
2. **Priests** held a leading place in ceremonies, leaving ordinary people little say.
3. **Sanskrit** was not understood by common people, while the new teachers used **Prakrit and Pali**.

questions.stem_md: Describe three social causes for the rise of Jainism and Buddhism.
questions.solution_md: Rigid varna; Kshatriyas; Vaishyas.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **varna system** had become rigid, with rank decided by birth.
2. **Kshatriyas** wished for a standing that matched their power.
3. Wealthy **Vaishyas** wanted respect that birth did not give them, so teachings open to all groups attracted them.

questions.stem_md: A label at an imagined exhibition says: born about 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali, and revered as the twenty-fourth Tirthankara. Whom does it describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Vardhamana Mahavira. Vardhamana Mahavira is the twenty-fourth Tirthankara. Siddhartha Gautama is the Buddha, Parshvanatha is counted as the twenty-third, and Bimbisara was a king.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined quiz held by the Ratnapur Junior Club, the host asks which Tirthankara is counted just before Mahavira. What is the answer?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Parshvanatha. Parshvanatha is counted as the twenty-third Tirthankara. Rishabhanatha is the first, the Buddha belongs to the Buddhist tradition, and Bimbisara was a king.

questions.stem_md: Neha, in an imagined Jain study circle, (A) trusts the teachings of the Tirthankaras, (B) studies them carefully and (C) lives by them in daily conduct. Which option matches A, B and C with the Tri-ratnas?

options.text_md: A: right conduct; B: right faith; C: right knowledge
A: right knowledge; B: right conduct; C: right faith
A: right faith; B: right conduct; C: right knowledge
A: right faith; B: right knowledge; C: right conduct

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A: right faith; B: right knowledge; C: right conduct. Trust is right faith, careful study is right knowledge and living by the teachings is right conduct. The other options mix these up.

questions.stem_md: Kamala, an imagined shopkeeper, finds that a customer left a silver coin behind by mistake and hurries after him to return it. Which Jain vow does her act best reflect?

options.text_md: Asteya, not taking what is not given

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Asteya, not taking what is not given. Returning what belongs to another is asteya. Ahimsa is about harm, brahmacharya is about restraint, and aparigraha is about limiting possessions.

questions.stem_md: Harishankar, an imagined landowner, gives away the extra grain stored in his barns and keeps only what his household needs. Which vow does this show?

options.text_md: Asteya, not taking what is not given

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Aparigraha, limiting attachment to possessions. Giving up surplus holdings is aparigraha. Satya concerns truth, ahimsa concerns harm, and asteya concerns not taking what belongs to others.

questions.stem_md: A student in the imagined Class IX-A writes that Parshvanatha taught four vows and a fifth was added by the twenty-fourth Tirthankara. Which vow was added?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Brahmacharya. The four taught earlier were ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha. Brahmacharya was the fifth, added by Mahavira.

questions.stem_md: A visitor to the imagined town of Sundarpur notices a Jain monk gently brushing the ground before each step. Which principle does this show?

options.text_md: Ahimsa, extended even to the smallest living beings
Asteya, not taking what is not given

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Ahimsa, extended even to the smallest living beings. Brushing the path to avoid harming tiny creatures expresses ahimsa. The other vows concern stealing, truth and possessions.

questions.stem_md: Ishaan, an imagined student, asks why Jains say that a person's deeds matter even after death. Which answer matches Jain teaching?

options.text_md: Deeds matter only if a priest performs a ritual afterwards
Actions bind karma to the soul, which shapes rebirth until the soul is freed
Deeds do not matter, because the soul is never affected
Deeds matter only to the king of the land

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Actions bind karma to the soul, which shapes rebirth until the soul is freed. In Jain belief actions attach karma to the soul and shape rebirth until the soul is freed. Rituals by others, indifference or royal concern are not Jain explanations.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Jain monks of the imagined town of Sundarpur sweep the ground before they walk.

**Reason (R):** Jain teaching holds that even very small creatures have souls and should not be harmed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Because every living being is held to have a soul, even tiny creatures are protected, which explains the practice.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Jainism, moksha is gained mainly through costly sacrifices performed by priests.

**Reason (R):** Jain teaching holds that liberation comes through right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: Jainism does not rely on costly sacrifices for moksha. R is true: the Tri-ratnas are the path to liberation.

questions.stem_md: An imagined monk of the Sundarpur monastery practises each vow below. Match each vow with a way of practising it.

match_right.text_md: Refusing to harm even a small insect
Taking nothing that is not given
Speaking truthfully even when it is hard

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Ahimsa is not harming, satya is truth, asteya is not taking what is not given, aparigraha is limiting possessions.

questions.stem_md: Name the Tri-ratnas of Jainism and say what the three together lead to.
questions.solution_md: Three jewels; they lead to moksha.

answer.model_answer_md: **Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct** are the three jewels, or Tri-ratnas. Together they are the path by which the soul is freed from karma and reaches **moksha**.

marking_scheme.step: Right faith, right knowledge, right conduct

questions.stem_md: Zoya, an imagined student, asks how karma is linked to rebirth in Jain belief. Explain briefly.
questions.solution_md: Karma shapes rebirth until moksha.

answer.model_answer_md: In Jain belief every **action** attaches **karma** to the soul. This karma decides the soul's **next birth**, so the soul is reborn again and again until it is freed from karma and attains **moksha**.

marking_scheme.step: Actions bind karma to the soul

questions.stem_md: How did Jain teachings reflect a belief in equality? Give two points.
questions.solution_md: Souls in all beings; open to all groups.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Jain teaching holds that **every living being has a soul**, so all deserve care.
2. The path to liberation was open to **people of every group**; **conduct**, and not birth, decided progress.

marking_scheme.step: Every living being has a soul
Path open to all; conduct not birth

questions.stem_md: Name the five Jain vows and say which of them was added by Mahavira.
questions.solution_md: Five vows; brahmacharya added.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The five vows are **ahimsa** (non-violence), **satya** (truth), **asteya** (not stealing), **aparigraha** (non-attachment) and **brahmacharya** (self-restraint).
2. Parshvanatha had already taught the first four vows to his followers before the time of Mahavira.
3. **Brahmacharya**, or self-restraint, was the vow that Mahavira added, so the number became five.

marking_scheme.step: First four taught earlier by Parshvanatha

questions.stem_md: Write three facts about Vardhamana Mahavira.
questions.solution_md: Birth; kevala jnana; Tirthankara.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He was born about **540 BCE** at **Kundagrama** near Vaishali.
2. After years of austere practice he attained **kevala jnana**, or perfect knowledge, and was called **Jina**, the conqueror, and **Mahavira**.
3. He is revered as the **twenty-fourth Tirthankara**, after Parshvanatha, and taught the five vows.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined pilgrimage diary, Kavya writes that her group stood at a place near Varanasi where the Buddha is traditionally said to have given his first sermon. Which place is it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Sarnath. The first sermon is traditionally placed at Sarnath. Lumbini is the birthplace, Kushinagar is where he passed away, and Bodh Gaya is where he attained enlightenment.

questions.stem_md: An imagined monk teaches that sickness, loss and old age touch every life. Which of the Four Noble Truths does this idea match?

options.text_md: The second: desire is the cause of suffering
The third: suffering can come to an end
The fourth: the Eightfold Path is the way

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The first: life involves suffering. The first truth says that life involves suffering. The second names desire as the cause, the third says suffering can end, and the fourth gives the way.

questions.stem_md: Arnav, an imagined schoolboy, feels unhappy each time a friend gets a new toy, because he keeps wanting more. Which Noble Truth does this illustrate?

options.text_md: The Eightfold Path leads to wealth
Desire is the cause of suffering
Suffering can be ended only by being born rich

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Desire is the cause of suffering. Constant wanting making him unhappy illustrates the second truth, that desire is the cause of suffering. The other options contradict Buddhist teaching.

questions.stem_md: Sana, an imagined student, decides to speak only truthfully and kindly and to avoid gossip. Which step of the Eightfold Path does this match?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Right speech. Truthful and kind words are right speech. Right livelihood concerns earning a living, right view concerns understanding, and right concentration concerns training the mind.

questions.stem_md: An imagined traveller says he tried a life of great luxury, then went without food for weeks, and found that neither helped his peace of mind. Which approach would the Middle Path recommend?

options.text_md: Avoiding both extreme indulgence and extreme self-denial

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Avoiding both extreme indulgence and extreme self-denial. The Middle Path avoids both extremes. Extreme indulgence and extreme self-denial are the two things it avoids, and it does not ask people to avoid every teacher.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student writes that Nirvana is a rich kingdom reached after death. How should the answer be corrected?

options.text_md: Nirvana is the name of the Buddha's birthplace
Nirvana is a council held at Valabhi
Nirvana is the code of rules for monks
Nirvana is freedom from desire and from the cycle of rebirth, bringing suffering to an end

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Nirvana is freedom from desire and from the cycle of rebirth, bringing suffering to an end. Nirvana is release from desire and rebirth, which ends suffering. It is not a place such as the birthplace, a council, or the rules of the Vinaya.

questions.stem_md: A diorama in an imagined museum at Bodhipur shows figures in simple robes sitting together to study and to follow rules of conduct. What does the group represent?

options.text_md: The Samiti, an assembly of the tribe
The Sangha, the community of Buddhist monks and nuns
The Tirthankaras, the ford-makers of Jainism
The Angas, a set of Jain texts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Sangha, the community of Buddhist monks and nuns. A community of robed monks following rules is the Sangha. The Samiti is a tribal assembly, the Tirthankaras are Jain teachers, and the Angas are texts, not a group.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Buddha is traditionally said to have given his first sermon at Sarnath.

**Reason (R):** The Buddha is traditionally said to have attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but the place of enlightenment does not explain the place of the first sermon; they are two separate events.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Buddhist teaching, Nirvana means freedom from desire and from the cycle of rebirth.

**Reason (R):** Nirvana means being reborn into a wealthy family.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: Nirvana is release from rebirth, so it cannot mean being reborn.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined Class IX poster says that the Middle Path of the Buddha asks followers to avoid both extreme indulgence and extreme self-denial.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The Middle Path is a balanced way between the two extremes.

questions.stem_md: On an imagined school trip, the guide says that the Buddha gave his first sermon at ___.
questions.solution_md: The first sermon is traditionally placed at Sarnath.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined quiz the host says that the path taught by the Buddha to end suffering is made of ___ steps.
questions.solution_md: The path has eight steps, which is why it is called the Eightfold Path.

questions.stem_md: A teacher in an imagined classroom at Bodhipur writes the Four Noble Truths on cards. Match each truth with its meaning.

match_right.text_md: The Eightfold Path is the way
Desire is the cause of suffering
Suffering can come to an end

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The truths in order: suffering, its cause, its end, and the way.

questions.stem_md: A tour guide in an imagined study tour names four sites. Match each site with the event traditionally linked with it.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Birth at Lumbini, enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath, mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar.

questions.stem_md: A guide on an imagined study tour arranges the stops in the order of events in the Buddha's life. Arrange them.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (b) → (d). Birth, enlightenment, first sermon, mahaparinirvana.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these four steps of the Eightfold Path in the order in which they are traditionally listed.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). View, speech, livelihood, concentration.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: List the eight steps of the Eightfold Path.
questions.solution_md: Eight steps.

answer.model_answer_md: **Right view, right resolve, right speech and right action**, followed by **right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration**. These eight steps form the way to end suffering.

questions.stem_md: What did the Buddha mean by Nirvana?
questions.solution_md: Freedom from desire and rebirth.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nirvana** is the state of **freedom from desire**, which the Buddha taught is the cause of suffering. It also means release from the **cycle of rebirth**, so that suffering comes to an end.

marking_scheme.step: Release from the cycle of rebirth

questions.stem_md:
The school archive of the imagined town of Ratnapur holds copies of the texts of two faiths.

(i) Name the Jain texts and the Buddhist texts held there, and the language of the Buddhist texts. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the three Pitakas of the Tripitakas. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the Jatakas and the Angas help a historian, and state one caution. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Texts named; Pitakas described; use and caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Jain texts are the **Angas**, twelve in tradition, compiled at the Council of Valabhi about the fifth to sixth century CE. The Buddhist texts are the **Tripitakas** and the **Jatakas**; the Tripitakas were composed in **Pali**.

(ii) The **Vinaya Pitaka** has rules for monks and nuns, the **Sutta Pitaka** has discourses attributed to the Buddha, and the **Abhidhamma Pitaka** has deeper analysis of the teachings.

(iii) The Angas and the Tripitakas preserve the **teachings and practices** of the faiths, while the Jatakas, set among merchants and villagers, give glimpses of **everyday life**. As the texts were first **handed down orally** and compiled later, and have a religious purpose, a historian reads them **with other sources**.

questions.stem_md:
In the sixth century BCE people of northern India listened with growing interest to new teachers such as Mahavira and the Buddha.

(i) State three religious causes for the rise of Jainism and Buddhism. **[3]**
(ii) Explain two social causes and one economic cause. **[3]**
(iii) How did the political situation and the use of local languages help the new faiths to spread? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Religious causes; social and economic causes; politics and language.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Rituals and sacrifices had become **complex and costly**; **priests** had a leading place in ceremonies; and **Sanskrit**, the language of the rites, was **not understood** by ordinary people.

(ii) Socially, the **varna system** had become rigid and birth-based, and **Kshatriyas** and **Vaishyas** wished for a higher standing. Economically, farming needed **cattle**, so large animal sacrifices worried farmers, who welcomed **ahimsa**.

(iii) New **kingdoms**, such as those of Magadha, grew strong, and their rulers **supported** the new teachers with gifts and protection. The teachers spoke **Prakrit and Pali**, which people understood, so the message **reached many more**. These teachings questioned some practices, while the older tradition continued.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Rise of kingdoms and royal support

questions.stem_md:
At an imagined meeting in the town hall of Kosalapur, three people speak: Dhanapal, a rich trader, Gopal, a farmer who needs every ox for ploughing, and Prince Raghav, a Kshatriya noble who admires a travelling teacher.

(i) Name the cause of the rise of new faiths that each speaker best represents. **[3]**
(ii) Explain why it mattered that the teacher spoke in the language of the people. **[3]**
(iii) A listener says that the new faiths arose only because people rejected the older tradition. Evaluate this view. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Causes matched to speakers; value of local language; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Dhanapal** shows the **economic and social** cause: trade made Vaishyas rich, and they wanted a higher standing. **Gopal** shows the **economic** cause: farming needed cattle, so he welcomed **ahimsa**. **Prince Raghav** shows the **social and political** cause: Kshatriyas wanted standing, and rulers supported teachers.

(ii) The **common language** meant that ordinary people could **understand** the teacher without a learned person to explain, so the teaching reached **more people** than Sanskrit would have.

(iii) The view is **only partly fair**. The new teachers **questioned** some practices, but many causes worked together: **social, economic and political** changes as well as religious ones. The older tradition **continued** alongside, so it was not simply a rejection.

questions.stem_md:
A teacher at an imagined Jain study camp near Sundarpur explains the main ideas of Mahavira.

(i) Name and explain the Tri-ratnas. **[3]**
(ii) Name the five vows. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the Jain ideas of karma, equality and moksha. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Tri-ratnas; five vows; karma, equality, moksha.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Tri-ratnas** are **right faith**, trust in the teachings; **right knowledge**, careful understanding of them; and **right conduct**, living by them.

(ii) The five vows are **ahimsa** (non-violence), **satya** (truth), **asteya** (not stealing), **aparigraha** (limiting possessions) and **brahmacharya** (self-restraint), the last added by Mahavira.

(iii) By the idea of **karma**, every action attaches karma to the soul and shapes rebirth. The belief in **equality** holds that all living beings have souls and that people of every group may follow the path. **Moksha** is liberation, when the soul is freed from karma and the cycle of birth through the Tri-ratnas and effort.

questions.stem_md:
In an imagined school play at Sundarpur, Mahavira is shown as a young man who leaves home to seek knowledge. In later scenes a shopkeeper returns a coin left by mistake, a landowner gives away surplus grain and a monk brushes the path before walking.

(i) Write three facts about Mahavira. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how karma, rebirth and moksha are linked in Jain teaching. **[3]**
(iii) Name the vow shown in each of the three later scenes and explain it. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Facts about Mahavira; karma, rebirth, moksha; vows in the scenes.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Mahavira was born about **540 BCE** at **Kundagrama** near Vaishali. He left home, and after years of austere practice he attained **kevala jnana**, or perfect knowledge, and was called **Jina**, the conqueror, and **Mahavira**. He is revered as the **twenty-fourth Tirthankara**, after Parshvanatha, and he taught the five vows.

(ii) Actions attach **karma** to the soul, and karma shapes the next birth, so the soul is **reborn** again and again. When karma is shed through the Tri-ratnas, that is right faith, right knowledge and right conduct, together with discipline, the soul reaches **moksha**, liberation from the cycle of birth.

(iii) The shopkeeper practises **asteya**, which means not taking what is not given. The landowner practises **aparigraha**, which means limiting possessions and attachment. The monk practises **ahimsa**, which means avoiding harm even to tiny creatures.

questions.stem_md:
A guide at an imagined museum of Buddhist teaching at Bodhipur asks visitors to explain the main ideas of the Buddha.

(i) State the Four Noble Truths. **[3]**
(ii) List the eight steps of the Eightfold Path. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the Middle Path and the idea of Nirvana, and name the community that preserved the teachings. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Four truths; eight steps; Middle Path, Nirvana, Sangha.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **first** truth is that life involves suffering. The **second** is that desire is the cause of suffering. The **third** is that suffering can come to an end. The **fourth** is that the Eightfold Path is the way to end it.

(ii) The eight steps are **right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration**. Together they guide a person in understanding, conduct and the training of the mind.

(iii) The **Middle Path** avoids both extreme indulgence and extreme self-denial, and follows a balanced course between them. **Nirvana** is freedom from desire and from the cycle of rebirth, and so the end of suffering. The teachings were kept alive by the **Sangha**, the community of monks and nuns, who followed the rules and shared the message with ordinary people.

questions.stem_md:
Two student groups in an imagined school at Kaveripur prepare a chart comparing Jainism and Buddhism.

(i) Give three similarities. **[3]**
(ii) Give three differences. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why a trader and a farmer of the sixth century BCE could both be attracted to these teachings, without ranking one faith above the other. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Similarities; differences; appeal to trader and farmer.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Both arose in the **sixth century BCE**, **questioned costly rituals**, accepted **karma and rebirth**, taught **ahimsa** and used **Prakrit and Pali**.

(ii) Jainism stresses **strict ahimsa and austerity**, with the **Tri-ratnas and five vows**; Buddhism teaches the **Middle Path**, the **Four Noble Truths** and the **Eightfold Path**. Buddhism spread to many lands, while Jainism stayed mainly in India.

(iii) A **trader** gained from trade and wished for a standing based on conduct, and both teachings valued conduct above birth. A **farmer** needed cattle and welcomed **ahimsa**. Both faiths offered these appeals in a similar way, so each can be studied on its own merits, with no ranking.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Appeal to the farmer; no ranking
